subtype: Approach: learn basic first aid and keep emergency numbers ready [Thinking]
passage: Three weeks after the crash outside her rented room in Pune, Hansa still replayed it: the stalled scooter, the shouting, her own hands doing nothing. On Saturday morning she opened a laptop at the kitchen counter. "I keep thinking I didn't know what to do," she told her flatmate Sahil. "What if next time I did?" She found a first-aid class taught by certified trainers at a recognised body and booked a seat for the following weekend. Then she picked up her phone and saved 112, the ambulance line and the nearest police station under names she could find in a second. "Panic makes you slow," she muttered. "Numbers ready, skills learned, and then it's a job, not a wall." Sahil pinned the same contacts on his own phone.

qa.q: Which numbers did Hansa save on her phone?
qa.a: She saved 112, the ambulance line and the nearest police station.

qa.q: What is Hansa still feeling three weeks after the crash?
qa.a: Hansa feels shaken and a little guilty about her hands doing nothing, and she wants to feel prepared.

qa.q: What else could Hansa do to stay ready, and why?
qa.a: Hansa could practise the course skills with Sahil now and then and check the saved contacts, because skills fade if they are never used.

qa.q: How might Sahil see Hansa's plan?
qa.a: Sahil probably sees it as sensible and reassuring, which is why he pinned the same contacts on his own phone.

grounding: Illustrates booking a certified first-aid course and saving emergency numbers after an incident so a frightening moment feels manageable next time.

subtype: Approach: report to the police and insurer with the right documents [Action]
passage: Sit, Indu, and let me tell you about the winter I was twenty-one. I'm Madhav. I was driving my father's car when a truck jumped a signal and hit us on the side. Nobody died, but my father's arm was broken and I couldn't think straight. Even so, I made myself do the boring things. That night I went to the police station and filed a report; the constable copied my licence and the papers. Next morning I rang the insurer, because the policy said to tell them within a fixed time. Then I put everything in one folder: the photos I had taken of the car, the hospital bills, the copy of the report. Months later the claim moved without a single argument, because every paper was there. The boring things helped us more than being brave did.

qa.q: What did Madhav keep in the folder?
qa.a: The folder held the photos of the car, the hospital bills and the copy of the report.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling at the crash scene?
qa.a: Madhav was shaken and overwhelmed, unable to think straight, yet pushed on with the practical tasks.

qa.q: Which choice in the story protected the claim, and why?
qa.a: Madhav filed the police report that night and rang the insurer next morning, because the policy set a time limit and the papers showed what had happened.

qa.q: How might Madhav's father have seen those first hours?
qa.a: Madhav's father, with a broken arm, was probably in pain and grateful that Madhav took care of the paperwork.

grounding: Illustrates filing a police report, informing the insurer in time and keeping bills and photos after a serious collision.

subtype: Approach: leave the scene out of fear [Pitfall]
passage:
Counselling note, Thursday. Lalremsiami came in after the police traced the car through a camera near the bus stand. The story came in short bursts: a pedestrian had stepped out at dusk, the bumper caught the person's leg, a crowd shouted and closed in, Lalremsiami's mind went white and the car drove off without stopping. The pedestrian sat by the road until a passer-by phoned for an ambulance. "If I'd stayed, it would have been a small thing," Lalremsiami kept saying. Now there is an added complaint for leaving, the pedestrian's family is angry, and Lalremsiami has stopped sleeping. I listened and did not argue, but said that being afraid is not the same as the matter being over. I can't advise on legal questions, so I gave the details of the legal aid clinic and offered to sit with Lalremsiami when facing the family.

Preeti, counsellor

qa.q: How did the police trace the car?
qa.a: The police traced the car through a camera near the bus stand.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when the crowd closed in?
qa.a: Lalremsiami was frightened and panicked, and the mind went white.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami have done instead of driving off, and why?
qa.a: Lalremsiami could have stayed, called for an ambulance and the police, and let them manage the angry crowd, because staying gets help to the injured person and stops the trouble from growing.

qa.q: How might the pedestrian have felt sitting by the road?
qa.a: The pedestrian was probably hurt and abandoned, waiting until a passer-by phoned for an ambulance.

grounding: Illustrates a driver panicking at a crowd and fleeing after hitting a pedestrian, leaving the injured person without help and adding trouble.

subtype: Approach: follow official warnings and evacuation orders [Action]
passage:
Sunday night. The rumour groups say the river will stay under the bridge, but the district authority's alert has gone from orange to red, and the weather department bulletin promises heavy rain for three more days. I checked both twice. Nandini from next door says her uncle claims the water never reaches our lane. I packed a bag anyway, told Amma, and walked with Nandini to the designated shelter at the government school before ten, showing our ID cards at the door. By midnight the corridor smelled of wet rope and dal. At five this morning the volunteers announced that the bridge road was closed. I'm so glad we did not wait.

Nilesh

qa.q: Where did Nilesh and Nandini go on Sunday night?
qa.a: They walked to the designated shelter at the government school.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when the volunteers announced the bridge road was closed?
qa.a: Nilesh felt relieved and glad that they had not waited.

qa.q: What else could Nilesh do to help neighbours, and why?
qa.a: Nilesh could share the official alert with neighbours who follow the rumour groups, because a clear message from a trusted source can help others decide early.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt about going early?
qa.a: Nandini may have felt unsure, since her uncle said the water never reaches the lane, but trusted the official alert enough to go along.

grounding: Illustrates a student in a flood-prone river town following official alerts and moving early to a designated shelter.

subtype: Approach: prepare a go-bag and family meeting point in advance [Action]
passage: Colony flood-preparedness note, Shankar (secretary). During Tuesday's door-to-door visit I stopped at flat 4B. Anand, a third-year student, showed me a blue waterproof bag by the door: the family's papers in a sealed pouch, a torch, a power bank already charged, four bottles of water and a small pack of the medicines the family uses regularly. On the fridge was a card with the meeting place, the temple gate at the end of the lane, and two phone numbers. Anand had gone over it at dinner so that everyone knew. When I asked why, Anand said, "If the water comes at night I don't want to be deciding what to grab." I have asked Anand to speak at Sunday's meeting, and next week I will photograph the list for the notice board.

qa.q: Where is the family's meeting place?
qa.a: The meeting place is the temple gate at the end of the lane.

qa.q: What was Anand worried about, judging by what Anand said?
qa.a: Anand was worried about being rushed and confused at night, and preferred to have the decisions made in advance.

qa.q: What could Shankar do to spread this practice, and why?
qa.a: Shankar could have Anand speak at the meeting and put the list on the notice board, because neighbours may follow a practical example from someone who has already done it.

qa.q: How might the family have experienced Anand's preparation?
qa.a: The family was probably reassured, since the plan was talked over at dinner and everyone knows where to go.

grounding: Illustrates packing documents, light, power, water and medicines in a waterproof bag and agreeing on a family meeting place ahead of a flood.

subtype: Approach: wait and see because it may not be serious [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Tanuja, and I live upstairs from Hrithik. Twice this monsoon the town had flood warnings, and twice the water stopped at the road. So on Monday, when the siren went again, I packed a bag and knocked on Hrithik's door. "Same as last time, it'll pass," Hrithik said, and turned the television up. By evening the drain outside was gurgling. At nine the water was over the doorstep, and by ten the lane to the main road had vanished under brown water and nobody could leave. Hrithik carried a suitcase up to my flat and stood on the stairs with a phone in hand, saying nothing. Downstairs the mattress and books were already soaked and the power was out. I felt sick watching the water climb. I don't know what was in Hrithik's mind. I only know the earlier warnings had been harmless.

qa.q: At what time was the water over the doorstep?
qa.a: At nine the water was over the doorstep.

qa.q: What might Hrithik have been thinking when saying it would pass?
qa.a: Hrithik probably felt calm and a little dismissive, since earlier warnings passed with little harm, though Tanuja can only guess.

qa.q: What could Hrithik have done differently, and why?
qa.a: Hrithik could have left with Tanuja when the siren first went, because a warning that ended harmlessly before does not mean the next will, and routes get cut once the water rises.

qa.q: What was it like for Tanuja to watch Hrithik stay behind?
qa.a: Tanuja felt worried and helpless, sick as the water climbed while Hrithik stayed put.

grounding: Illustrates staying put because earlier warnings passed harmlessly and leaving only after water enters the ground floor and routes are cut.

subtype: Approach: scenario planning for power and phone loss [Thinking]
passage:
Gopika: Okay, imagine the cyclone knocks out the towers and the power. Two days, no phone. What do we do?
Irawati: Charge everything tonight?
Gopika: A power bank helps, but say it dies too. Then what?
Irawati: Then... I only know my brother's number by heart, and that's because it never changed.
Gopika: So we write numbers on paper. Warden, both our families, the ward office, the clinic. Tape the list inside the cupboard door.
Irawati: The caretaker has a small radio. I'll ask if we can borrow it.
Gopika: Good. And we download an offline map of the way to the school shelter tonight.
Irawati: Who calls whom?
Gopika: Whoever finds signal first calls your brother in Nagpur, and he tells everyone else. One person outside the city.
Irawati: Fine, I'll warn him now. Nothing fancy, just what the phones can't do.

qa.q: Where will the paper list of numbers be kept?
qa.a: The list will be taped inside the cupboard door.

qa.q: What does Irawati's remark about knowing only one number by heart suggest about how Irawati feels?
qa.a: It suggests Irawati feels a little uneasy and exposed, since the phone holds nearly all the contacts.

qa.q: What else could Gopika and Irawati agree on, and why?
qa.a: They could agree a fixed meeting point in case the hostel is unsafe, because without phones they cannot message each other to find one another.

qa.q: How might Irawati's brother in Nagpur see his part in the plan?
qa.a: He would probably feel responsible and a little anxious, since he is the one outside contact who passes messages to everyone.

grounding: Illustrates imagining two days without power and phones and planning a paper list, a radio or offline map, and who contacts whom.

subtype: Approach: help neighbours through community coordination [Action]
passage:
Madhav: After you reached the school shelter, what did you do?

Maria: Honestly? Sat on a mat for one night. Then I saw a notice: the local volunteer group needed hands. I signed up, and the ward officer gave us a list of elders living alone. We didn't wade anywhere. The officer told us which lanes were safe, and the boats went to the others. My job was carrying dal and rice packets and knocking on doors with a checklist. We ticked each name, noted who needed the health volunteer to visit, and handed the sheet back to the officer at the end of the day. At first I wanted to run to the worst lane myself. I was impatient and wanted to do something big. It turned out to be better that we worked as a group, and every name got a visit.

qa.q: What did the ward officer give the volunteers?
qa.a: The ward officer gave the volunteers a list of elders living alone.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when wanting to run to the worst lane?
qa.a: Maria felt impatient and eager to do something big, but accepted the group plan.

qa.q: What could go wrong if volunteers each went alone, and what works better?
qa.a: Lone volunteers could end up in unsafe lanes and miss people, while working with the officer covers more homes safely.

qa.q: How might an elder living alone see the volunteers' visit?
qa.a: The elder would probably feel relieved and cared for, being checked on by someone with a list and food rather than being forgotten.

grounding: Illustrates a student joining a volunteer group and working with authorities to deliver food and check on elders after reaching safety.

subtype: Approach: go back too early to save belongings [Pitfall]
passage: The water outside the camp had dropped by a hand's width, and Yamini could not stop thinking about the laptop and the folder of certificates on her bed. The volunteer at the camp had said to wait until the authorities cleared the lane. "One trip. Twenty minutes," she told Pooja, her flatmate. Pooja begged her not to go. At the lane the water was still knee-deep and brown, its current tugging at her legs. The ground floor was dark, the electricity off. On the stairs a floating board slid under her foot and she went down, cutting her palm on the railing. In the dusk she grabbed the laptop bag and one wet folder. A volunteer in a boat shouted at her to stop and pulled her aboard. Pooja was crying at the camp gate. The laptop never switched on again.

qa.q: What did Yamini hurt on the railing?
qa.a: She hurt her palm, cutting it on the railing.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling as she thought about her laptop and certificates?
qa.a: Yamini was anxious about losing her things, so anxious that fear of the loss beat her caution.

qa.q: What could Yamini have done instead, and why?
qa.a: Yamini could have asked the camp volunteers about collecting the papers once the lane was cleared, because belongings can be replaced but she cannot.

qa.q: How did Pooja see Yamini's trip?
qa.a: Pooja was frightened and helpless, begging Yamini not to go and crying at the camp gate.

grounding: Illustrates returning to a flooded home too early against advice to save a laptop and documents, risking safety through attachment to things.

subtype: Approach: rumours and forwarded messages shape decisions [Pitfall]
passage:
Mehak: Anand!! Forward from the ward group: DAM HAS BURST, RUN TO HIGH GROUND NOW 😰
Mehak: Papa's already taking the car out
Anand: Wait. Who sent it first?
Mehak: Uncle from the group. Someone sent it to him.
Anand: There's no time or place in it. Checking the district site and the water department page.
Anand: Both say the gates are being watched. Nothing about a breach. The alert says stay off the bridge road.
Mehak: But everybody's driving that way to the highway!
Anand: That's the road that's jammed. Tell Papa the official page says don't use it.
Mehak: ok calling him. He's stopping the car.
Anand: I'm not forwarding it on. Posted the official link in the group instead 🙂

qa.q: Which road did the official alert say to stay off?
qa.a: The alert said to stay off the bridge road.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when sending the forward?
qa.a: Mehak was panicked and in a hurry to get family to safety.

qa.q: What else could Anand do to reduce panic, and why?
qa.a: Anand could add a short line to the group that no breach is confirmed, because a clear correction with a source spreads as easily as a rumour.

qa.q: How might Mehak's papa have felt during all this?
qa.a: Papa was probably alarmed and protective, rushing to drive the family out, and then relieved to learn the road was jammed and the report unconfirmed.

grounding: Illustrates a widely shared unverified dam-burst message pushing people onto blocked roads while a student checks official channels and stops forwarding it.
